summary: Reserves the last Autonomous System Numbers in the 16-bit and 32-bit ranges and gives guidance on their use. It updates Section 10 of RFC 1930 and is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: This Best Current Practice reserves the last number in the 16-bit and 32-bit Autonomous System Number ranges. It explains how operators and BGP implementations should treat those numbers.

questions: should last asns be filtered in bgp
subtitle: A Best Current Practice reserving the last ASN in each number range and explaining how to handle them.

tldr.problem: The final ASNs in the 16-bit and 32-bit ranges are reserved, but could be mistaken for Private Use ASNs.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explains the reservations and tells operators not to use or globally advertise these numbers, while BGP implementations should not treat them as protocol errors.
tldr.outcome: The document reserves ASNs 65535 and 4294967295 and updates Section 10 of RFC 1930.

today: RFC 7300 is a Best Current Practice that updates RFC 1930. The unit metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes RFC 7300.

sections.title: The Reserved Last ASNs
sections.content:
The RFC calls the final number in each Autonomous System Number range a Last ASN. It identifies 65535 as the last 16-bit ASN and 4294967295 as the last 32-bit ASN.

Although these numbers border on Private Use ASN ranges, the RFC says they are not defined or reserved as Private Use ASNs. It updates Section 10 of RFC 1930.
sections.plainLanguage: The last number in each range is set aside. These numbers are not Private Use ASNs.

sections.title: Why the Numbers Are Reserved
sections.content:
Some BGP communities of ASN 65535 are reserved for Well-known Communities, as described in RFC 1997. The RFC says this is not then true of ASN 4294967295, but it could be a candidate for a future Special Use ASN that is not globally routable.

The RFC does not assign such a special use to ASN 4294967295.
sections.plainLanguage: ASN 65535 has a connection to reserved BGP community values. The other number is kept available as a possible candidate for future special use, but no use is assigned in this RFC.

sections.title: Guidance for Network Operators
sections.content:
Operators SHOULD NOT use Last ASNs for another purpose or as Private Use ASNs. The RFC warns that using AS 65535 as if it were private could accidentally invoke BGP Well-known Community values.

Last ASNs MUST NOT be advertised to the global Internet in AS_PATH or AS4_PATH attributes. Operators SHOULD filter them in those attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators should not assign these reserved numbers for ordinary use. They must not advertise them globally in the listed BGP path attributes.

sections.title: Guidance for BGP Implementations
sections.content:
The RFC says Last ASNs remain valid ASNs from BGP's perspective. Implementations SHOULD NOT treat them as protocol errors. If a Last ASN is configured as the local AS, an implementation MAY warn that a reserved ASN is being used.

Tools that filter Private Use ASNs in AS_PATH and AS4_PATH MAY also include Last ASNs. The RFC says it introduces no additional security concerns, though BGP implementation errors could be triggered by their use.
sections.plainLanguage: A BGP implementation should not treat a Last ASN as an invalid protocol value. It may warn if an operator configures one as the local ASN.
